Durban Vigilantism [5971]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Production

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Durban Riots and Vigilantism


Pres Ramaphosa in his family meeting admitted that we must admit that we did not have the capabilities and plans in place to respond swiftly and decisively.

In this political vacuum the public realised that they had to restore order and protect their communities. The police could not cope with the tsunami of looters and violence.
Across Durban residents mobilised and formed Community Police Forums. I have filmed them over 2 days in Durban. They gathered volunteers, and barricaded the roads to protect their residents and assets.
They tried to secure their food and fuel sources.

Technology helped with this. Many used an app called Zello which turned their cell phones into a mobile 2 way radio, transmitting to which ever resident was tuned into the channel.
In the beginning one can hear the panic in people’s voices and many were calling for arms and ammunition. I can get recordings of this.

I have filmed Reservoir Hills patrol and interviewed KE8 trauma doctor Kevin Naidu and Dash Singh who heads up the Durban North CPF. The people have galvanised and presented a
united force against the threat of looters to their areas. There was a lot of good in these initiatives.

Shortly after violent protests erupted at the weekend, Durban Mayor Mxolisi Kaunda posted on his Facebook page: “We are Msholozi, Msholozi is us. #Free Zuma.”

In the beginning there was no sense of how this would all pan out. Images of destruction were being broadcast 24/7 and the uncertainty caused tensions to rise.

This did create a breeding ground for vigilantism and people did take the law into their own hands. The barricades were manned by heavily guarded volunteers.
Roads were blocked with strips of wood studded with nails.

The unease raised racial tensions and some took the law into their own hands, especially the tension between the overzealous Indian patrollers in Phoenix and their neighbours in Bhambayi, Amaoti and Zwelisha. There are horrific scenes of looters being shot at and abused and the neighbouring black houses being set alight. They estimate that over 20 looters were killed by vigilantism.

Bheki Cele also went to the scene to try and calm the tempers down.

When food and petrol became scarce, the people on the barricades became more adamant to protect their resources and would not allow people to enter without proof of residents.
For many it reminded them of the dumps system.

There is a scene with a black couple that tried to come into an area and they are verbally abused by very aggressive residents.

The police commissioners then stopped anyone having barricades. The constitution allows for freedom of movement and all barricades have now gone.This caused the residents to feel exceptionally vulnerable and exposed.

But what do people do when there is no visible policing and their lives and properties are at risk.

Stock footage of Bheki Cele in Phoenix.

Interviews with
Lisette Lancaster ISS an expert on vigilantism OR
Mary de Haas violence monitor and social scientist
Umesh Singh the chairperson of the Phoenix Police Forum
Xolani Dube, founder of the Xubera Institute for Reattach and Development.

And then in contrast we have the rainbow nation side to our society. People came out in droves and volunteered to clean up the roads, food was being shipped in, the mosques were giving out free bread and
there was a general sense of bonhomie and camaraderie like the 95 World Cup.

I have interviews with two CPF leaders, Nicole Graham from DA who talks about political vacuum and she also volunteered at Musgrave CPF, two people cleaning streets after massacre, one community street patroller.

Dash Singh
Glen Naidoo

Script Durban Edit 10


V/O
Monday the 12th of July 2021 will be remembered as the day Durban burned.

That was almost two weeks ago, but there is still an acrid smell in the morning air fueled by the smouldering embers of the factories that were raised to the ground by looters. The streets looked post apocalyptic littered with glass and cardboard, the remnants of the cataclysmic assault on the city. The stark reality is that the looting caused billions of rands of damage , a death toll of over 250 people in KZN and estimated 130 000 jobs hang in the balance

When visiting the disaster zones last Friday President Cyril Ramaphosa admitted that they were overwhelmed by the situation and could have done better.

Ramaphosa
“As this government we must acknowledge that we were poorly prepared for an orchestrated public campaign of public violence, destruction and sabotage of this nature.
While we commend the brave actions of our security forces on the grounds we must admit that we did not have the capabilities and plans in place to respond swiftly and decisively.”

Up sounds of people lost businesses and stores

V/O
With a Police Force not able to contain the tsunami of looting, it became like a war zone, seeing the imminent threat to life and property most of Durban’s suburbs galvanized together to protect themselves. They mobilised into informal forums, assembled volunteers and patrolled borders to secure their food and fuel.

Dash Singh is from the newly formed Durban North Joint Operation

Dash
“We saw all the neighbouring suburbs starting to burn we saw them having drama and the shops being looted and we said that before it comes here we need to take firm action.”

Link
Several communities barricaded their neighbourhoods to prevent the looters from entering. Some of the patrollers were armed with hockey sticks , pangas knives , paintball guns and others with guns and live ammunition.

Mac
“Was it a concern that some of your members of community might be armed even though tensions were so high?”

Dash
“The community members were armed , if family is under threat I will take whatever steps I can take to protect them. Constitutionally one of the highest guaranteed rights is the right to life.”

Up sound.

I can see the situation escalting guys proceed with caution

V/O
Most of the neighbourhoods had little or no experience in dealing with these situations.
What they decided to do was to block access into their neighbourhoods with barricades.

V/O
Nicole Graham is a volunteer for the Community Patrol in Musgrave and says with stretched police resources what were the communities meant to do to protect themselves?

Nicole
“What we have been dong in our area is not necessarily stopping people but trying to narrow the road and restrict access in terms of making sure people have to be driving slowly and that we can have reasonable control and it has been successful because we have thwarted major crime attempts.

V/O
Dash Singh believes that even though they do not have the necessary experience, they had the tenacity to protect their boundaries.
After ransacking the malls, the looters made for other targets in the neighbourhoods and were thwarted by the community.

Dash
I live amongst the best people in the country , they came out in their thousands to come and help us, immediately when they heard, this community coalesced so quickly.

V/O
Trauma doctor Kevin Naidu heads up the Reservoir Hills community policing sub forum and after ransacking the mall the looters headed their way.

Kev
It is estimated that there were about 200 – 300 people heading towards us. And there was a lot of fear at that point. Even for myself, because we are not trained to do this here.

V/O
The residents managed to repel 3 attacks with thunder flashes and paint ball guns.

Kev
“We held this line over here and we said that we would not run away from our people.”


V/O
Technology has been a huge weapon in the neighbourhood watch arsonal. Zello is a phone app that was a game changer.

Link
It turns your phone into a walkie talkie that works anywhere in the world as long as you are connected to the internet.

Up Sound
Let me know where you are and I can be there in a few minutes.

V/O
Some communities also used thermal imaging drone footage to assess incoming threats

Up sound fridge driving in

The looting didn’t stop for days and the Durban Metro Police Service was overwhelmed and out numbered.

Up sound I have been waiting

Sbonelo Mchunu is the Deputy Commissioner and says that at any time they only can muster 400 Metro Police per shift.

Mchunu
“As far as the people were concerned they will be still be looting, they stopped looting because of the police, so we were there, we couldn’t be in every corner. The numbers don’t allow us.

V/O
But the barricades also created trauma for law abiding citizens.

Zithobile Matyhobo from Amaoti was held up a gun point in 4 separate road blocks by Phoenix vigilanties when she was taking a critically ill friend and her recently born baby to hospital.

Zithobile
“Where are you going, we are going to the hospital, we started crying on the road pleading for help, and let us move to the hospital. They were having big guns, bush knives. If you don’t want to come out of this van, we will kill you. Where are you going?”

V/O
Lizette Lancaster from the Institute for Security Studies is an expert in vigilantism, when people take the law into their own hands.

Lizette
The police were not there when many of these areas erupted.
This is where things went awry we saw people not only trying to protect themselves but also meting out punishment and that is what makes vigilantism such a concerning aspect in South African society.”

Up Sound
When we needed you, you wasn’t here, you wasn’t here for us.

Lizette
“Often in times of very emotionally charged situations, people over step the mark, and racially profile people or assault and that then just causes more mistrust.”

V/O
The memories of the violence still haunt Zithobile.

Sbonelo
“We lost 20 people in Phoenix because of the criminal element disguised as community, however we will also not undermine some communities that were very cooperating and working for the interest of society and we recommend those communities.”

“I chose to come here today to help the community.”

V/O
And out of the ashes that incredible South African spirit galvanized communities, they took to the streets and cleaned them up. Trucks came in and gave food freely to those in need. There is an apprehensive calm at the moment, the South African National Defence Force troops have been mobilized to maintain order, ring leaders have been arrested and thousands of other still face the might of the law. But the path back to stability in Durban is a long one.







Promo 1 x 11 secs
With little visible policing, Durban residents took up arms to protect themselves during last week’s looting. Is this the beginning of vigilantism or a justifiable response to protect life and limb?

Promo 2 x 21 secs

The Durban Metro Police had 400 members per shift to quell the uprising of the thousands in the recent riots. Residents realized that they would have to fend for themselves and came to the community’s defence with hockey sticks, pangas and paintball guns. When do you have the right to take the law into your own hands?

Promo 3 x 21 secs.

These are the remnants of the factories that were burnt in Durban looting , the buildings were raised to the ground but deep-seated divisions – economic and racial were ignited. With a lack of police presence neighbourhoods armed themselves to protect what they felt was theirs.







































These are the smouldering embers from the rampant looting in Durban which claimed According to preliminary reports compiled by NatJoints, extensive damage has been caused to 161 malls and shopping centres, 11 warehouses, 8 factories and 161 liquor outlets and distributors.
